title: Sudden sniffing death

claims.statement: In young people in the United States in the 1960s, sudden deaths right after sniffing volatile hydrocarbons (solvents and aerosol sprays), without suffocation in a plastic bag, were described in a series of 110 deaths gathered by a nationwide survey in 1969 whose methods are not described (Bass, 1970). Those who died were aged 11 to 23, and 37 were known to have sniffed before, occasionally or habitually; the products were mostly aerosol propellants (fluorocarbons; 59 deaths) and the cleaning solvent 1,1,1-trichloroethane (29), then toluene (8), benzene (7) and gasoline (4) (editors' sums of the paper's map); none was an alkyl nitrite (poppers). Where an autopsy is described, it found no anatomical cause of death; volatile hydrocarbons were found in the organs in 44 deaths (how many were tested is not given), so most deaths were attributed from the circumstances. In six eyewitness accounts the person suddenly ran, screamed or became agitated, or called out that his heart was stopping, just before collapsing; eight people dashed a few hundred feet and then collapsed; and an activity or stress, such as being surprised by parents or police, running from police, wrestling or riding a bicycle, was listed for 18 deaths. Family or friends hid the sniffing in 8 deaths. Products that animal inhalation tests had suggested were of low toxicity were among those involved. The author proposed that the hydrocarbons make the heart prone to a sudden fatal rhythm, set off by adrenaline from fright or exertion, drawing on cat and anaesthesia studies; no heart rhythm was recorded in any death, and he wrote that it is difficult to say what caused the panic before collapse. With no count of how many people sniffed, the series cannot say how often sniffing ends in sudden death or whether this was becoming more common (the abstract's 'sharp rise' in incidence has no rate behind it), and without sniffing episodes that did not end in death to compare with, it cannot show that fright or exertion raises the risk. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Bass (1970): 110 deaths; by chemical (editors' sums of Figure 2): aerosol fluorocarbon propellants 59, 1,1,1-trichloroethane 29, toluene 8, benzene 7, gasoline 4, toluene with trichloroethane 2, unidentified 1; by region West 57, Central 18, East 35; ages 11 to 23; history of occasional or habitual sniffing 37; activity or stress listed for 18 (16 in 100, editors' calculation, a lower bound of recorded circumstances, not a frequency); sudden dash before collapse in 8 witnessed deaths; volatile hydrocarbons found at toxicology in 44 (number tested not given), quantified in 12; sniffing concealed by family or friends in 8. No rate can be computed.
